title: Music · Episode 1
chapters: How music learned to be written down
Why every piano is slightly out of tune

units.t: Music. Episode one.
In this episode: How music works, How music learned to be written down, Why every piano is slightly out of tune and The world of instruments.
Part one. How music works.
Every song you love is just air, pushed back and forth in careful patterns.
Here is how those patterns become music.
Sound, pitch and frequency.
A vibrating guitar string squeezes and stretches the air beside it.
That pressure wave travels at about 343 metres per second, roughly a kilometre every three seconds, and nudges your eardrum.
Tiny bones pass the movement to the cochlea, where hair cells turn it into nerve signals.
Pitch depends on frequency, measured in hertz, Hz.
A healthy young ear hears roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, and the upper limit falls with age.
Orchestras tune to the A above middle C at 440 Hz.
Double any frequency and you get the same note an octave higher, so the next A is 880 Hz.
That's why men and women singing the 'same' tune are often an octave apart without noticing.
Why instruments sound different.
A piano and a violin can play exactly the same pitch and still sound completely different.
The reason is timbre, or tone colour.
Almost no instrument produces a single pure frequency.
Alongside the main note, the fundamental, it produces fainter overtones at higher frequencies, often simple multiples of the fundamental.
Each instrument has its own recipe of overtones, plus its own way of starting and fading a note: the sharp strike of a piano hammer, the smooth swell of a bowed string.
Your brain reads that recipe instantly, which is how you can recognise a familiar voice from a single word.
Rhythm and melody.
The beat is the pulse you tap your foot to, and tempo is its speed in beats per minute.
A slow ballad sits around 60 to 80, while much dance music runs at about 120 to 130.
Beats group into bars, commonly four beats, though waltzes use three.
Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds over that pulse.
Humans are unusually good at locking onto a beat; few other animals do, though some parrots have been filmed bobbing in time.
A melody is a line of notes your brain hears as one shape.
Good melodies repeat short motifs so you can follow them, then vary them to stay interesting.
Most move in small steps with occasional leaps, build to a high point, and settle back 'home', one of music's strongest pulls.
Scales and harmony.
Most Western music divides each octave into 12 equal steps called semitones, the white and black keys on a piano.
A scale is a chosen subset.
The major scale uses seven, the do-re-mi from school.
The pentatonic scale uses five and appears in folk music from Scotland to China to West Africa.
Indian classical and Arabic music use pitches between the piano's keys.
Harmony is notes sounding together.
Consonant combinations sound smooth and stable; dissonant ones sound tense.
Consonant intervals have simple frequency ratios: an octave is 2 to 1, and a perfect fifth, the interval opening many fanfares, is 3 to 2.
Much of music's drama comes from building tension with dissonance, then resolving it to a consonant chord.
Happy chords, sad chords.
Listeners raised on Western music usually hear major chords as bright or happy and minor chords as darker or sad.
The difference is small: in a minor chord, the middle note is one semitone lower.
Why it matters so much is still debated.
Some researchers point to acoustics, and to similarities with the way sad speech is lower and flatter.
Others stress learning, since the association varies between cultures and eras.
Context counts too: a minor key at a fast tempo can sound energetic rather than sad.
Next time a song moves you, listen for where the key or tempo changes.
The key idea: Sound is a pressure wave, and pitch is how we hear its frequency: faster vibrations sound higher.
Part two. How music learned to be written down.
For most of history, music lived only in memory.
The squiggles, lines and dots that now let anyone read a song were invented bit by bit over a thousand years.
Music without paper.
Every culture has made music, but very few wrote it down with precise pitches and rhythms.
Melodies were learned by listening and copying.
Some ancient societies did develop notation.
A clay tablet from the city of Ugarit, in modern Syria, dating to around 1400 BCE, contains instructions for a hymn, and the ancient Greeks used letter symbols for pitch.
But these systems were limited or lost.
In medieval Europe, the church's huge repertoire of chant, now often called Gregorian chant, was learned by heart.
Training a singer to know it all could take many years.
Neumes and the staff.
From around the ninth century, scribes added little marks called neumes above the Latin words in chant books.
They showed whether the melody rose or fell, but not exactly how high or how long.
They were memory aids: a singer who had never heard a chant could not learn it from neumes alone.
Gradually, scribes placed them at different heights, so position hinted at pitch.
Around 1030, the Italian monk Guido of Arezzo championed notes on horizontal lines, each representing a fixed pitch, with letters that became clefs.
Singers could now read a melody they had never heard, and Guido claimed young singers could learn in a short time what once took years.
Music could travel on parchment alone.
The origin of solfège.
Guido also gave singers a memory trick.
He used a Latin hymn to Saint John the Baptist in which each of the first six lines began one step higher than the last.
The first syllables of those lines were ut, re, mi, fa, sol and la.
By learning the hymn, students fixed the sound of each step in their minds.
Over the centuries, ut was replaced in most countries by do, which is easier to sing.
A seventh syllable, si, was added later, and in the nineteenth century English teachers changed it to ti so every syllable began with a different letter.
This system, called solfège, is still used to teach singing around the world.
Writing down time.
Showing pitch was only half the problem.
As composers wrote for several voices singing different lines at once, called polyphony, singers needed to know exactly how long each note lasted so they stayed together.
In the thirteenth century, theorists such as Franco of Cologne set out rules in which the shape of a note indicated its duration.
This system, called mensural notation, developed over the following centuries.
Notes gradually changed from black squares and diamonds to the round open and filled heads used today.
Bar lines became common only in the seventeenth century.
Time signatures, rests and ties followed.
Print and other systems.
Copying music by hand was slow and expensive.
In 1501, the Venetian printer Ottaviano Petrucci published the Odhecaton, generally regarded as the first book of polyphonic music printed with movable type.
Printed music spread compositions across Europe and created a market of amateurs who bought music to play at home.
Staff notation is not universal.
Renaissance lute players used tablature, which shows where to put the fingers rather than which notes sound, as modern guitar tabs do.
India, China, Indonesia and other traditions have their own systems, and many jazz, folk and popular musicians learn by ear.
Notation struggles to capture subtle timing, tone colour and improvisation.
In the twentieth century, some composers used graphic scores of drawings and instructions.
The key idea: For most of history, music was passed on by ear and memory, and early notation systems were limited or lost.
Part three. Why every piano is slightly out of tune.
Ancient thinkers noticed that beautiful harmonies follow simple number ratios.
Then musicians discovered those ratios don't quite fit together.
The compromise they reached shapes every song you hear.
Harmony is numbers.
Legend credits Pythagoras with noticing that musical harmony follows numbers, though the story of him hearing blacksmiths' hammers is almost certainly myth.
The basic discovery is real, and you can test it on a guitar.
Pluck an open string, then press it at the halfway point and pluck again: the note is an octave higher, because the vibrating length has halved and the frequency has doubled, a ratio of 2 to 1.
Press a third of the way along, so two thirds vibrates, and you get a perfect fifth, a ratio of 3 to 2, the interval at the start of many familiar tunes.
A ratio of 4 to 3 gives a perfect fourth, and 5 to 4 a major third.
Simple ratios sound smooth and stable together.
Why simple ratios sound sweet.
A string or voice sounds a note at its main frequency and also at whole-number multiples of it, faint higher tones called overtones that give each instrument its colour.
If two notes are in a simple ratio, many of their overtones line up exactly.
When two tones are close but not quite matched, they interfere and produce a regular wobble in loudness called beating.
Play two notes that differ by two cycles per second and you hear the sound pulse twice a second.
Piano tuners listen for exactly these beats, slowing or speeding them to set each interval.
Simple ratios produce little beating, so they sound calm and clear.
The unavoidable comma.
Here is the snag.
Start on C and go up by a pure fifth to G, then D, then A, and keep going.
After twelve fifths you have passed through every note and should land on a C, seven octaves above where you began.
But the numbers disagree.
Twelve pure fifths multiply out to about 129.
7 times the starting frequency, while seven octaves give exactly 128.
The gap is the Pythagorean comma.
Musicians measure intervals in cents, with 100 cents in a modern semitone and 1200 in an octave, and the comma is about 23.
5 cents, roughly a quarter of a semitone.
It is a mathematical fact: no keyboard can have all its fifths and octaves perfectly pure at once.
Wolves, meantone and Bach.
Pythagorean tuning kept fifths pure, but its major thirds sounded harsh.
Renaissance musicians adopted meantone temperaments, narrowing the fifths so the common major thirds came out pure or nearly so.
The leftover error piled up in one fifth that howled, called the wolf fifth.
Nearby keys sounded lovely, but distant keys were sour or unusable, and changing key could mean retuning.
By the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, musicians wanted every key.
Well temperaments spread the comma unevenly, so no interval howled, though common keys stayed sweeter and remote keys more tense, giving each key its own flavour.
In 1722 Bach completed the first book of The Well-Tempered Clavier, twenty-four preludes and fugues, one in every major and minor key.
Scholars still debate his tuning, but it was probably not modern equal temperament.
Equal temperament and beyond.
Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve exactly equal semitones, each a frequency ratio of the twelfth root of two, about 1.
Zhu Zaiyu in China worked it out in the late 1500s, as did Simon Stevin in Europe.
It became the piano standard in the nineteenth century, and every key now sounds the same.
The price is that almost every interval is slightly impure.
Fifths are about two cents narrow, but major thirds are about fourteen cents wider than the pure 5 to 4 ratio, a shimmer our ears accept as normal.
Choirs and string quartets tune thirds by ear so harmony rings.
Tuners stretch piano octaves a little wider because stiff strings run sharp.
Concert pitch sets the A above middle C at 440 cycles per second.
Gamelan and Arabic music use scales that fall between piano keys.
The key idea: Pleasing musical intervals correspond to simple ratios, which you can test by pressing a guitar string.
Part four. The world of instruments.
Blow, bow, pluck, strike or switch it on: every instrument ever made uses one of a handful of tricks to shake the air.
Five kinds of vibration.
In 1914, musicologists Erich von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs published a system for sorting instruments by what actually vibrates.
Idiophones vibrate their whole body, like bells, rattles and xylophones.
Membranophones use a stretched skin, like most drums.
Chordophones use strings, from the harp to the guitar.
Aerophones vibrate a column of air, like flutes, trumpets and the didgeridoo.
A fifth group, electrophones, was added later for instruments that make sound electronically.
Museums still use this system because it works for instruments from any culture, not just the European orchestra.
Strings and the piano.
A vibrating string moves very little air, so stringed instruments use a hollow wooden body to resonate and amplify it.
Players change pitch by string length, a finger on the neck shortens it, tension, tuning pegs, and thickness, heavier strings sound lower.
Violins, cellos and double basses are bowed, with horsehair coated in rosin to grip.
Guitars, harps and lutes are plucked.
The piano is a stringed instrument too.
Before it, the harpsichord plucked strings at much the same volume however hard you pressed.
Around 1700 in Florence, Bartolomeo Cristofori built keys that threw leather-covered hammers at the strings, so pressing harder made a louder note.
Pianoforte means 'soft-loud'.
Today's piano has an iron frame and 88 keys.
Wind and brass.
Wind instruments set a column of air vibrating inside a tube, and the tube's length sets the pitch.
Woodwinds start the vibration in two main ways.
A flute player blows across an edge, like blowing over a bottle.
Clarinets and saxophones use a single cane reed, and oboes and bassoons use a double reed.
Covering holes changes the tube's effective length.
Brass players buzz their lips into a cup-shaped mouthpiece, and valves or a slide add extra tubing to lower the pitch.
The family is defined by the lips, not the metal: the saxophone is brass-coloured, but it is a woodwind.
Drums to synthesisers.
Percussion instruments are struck, shaken or scraped, and are probably the oldest family, since clapping and hitting sticks need no technology.
Some are untuned, like snare drums, cymbals and shakers.
Others have definite pitches, like timpani, xylophones and the steel pans of Trinidad and Tobago, invented in the twentieth century from oil drums.
The theremin, invented by Leon Theremin around 1920, is played without touching it: your hands near two antennas change its pitch and volume.
In the 1960s Robert Moog's synthesisers let musicians shape sounds with knobs and cables.
Australia's CSIRAC, one of the first stored-program computers, played music in the early 1950s.
Since 1983, MIDI has let keyboards and computers talk to each other, so a laptop can stand in for a studio.
The yidaki, with respect.
The instrument most Australians call the didgeridoo is the yidaki to the Yolŋu people of north-east Arnhem Land, with other names elsewhere.
It is traditionally a eucalyptus branch hollowed by termites.
Players buzz their lips for a deep drone and use circular breathing, breathing in through the nose while pushing air out from the cheeks.
Rock art suggests it has been played for at least a thousand years.
'Didgeridoo' is not an Aboriginal word and probably imitates the sound.
It accompanies ceremony, and its rhythms can link to clans, places and stories.
Protocols on making and playing it differ between communities; in some it is a men's role.
Buy from Aboriginal-owned makers and art centres, and learn the protocols from Aboriginal teachers.
The key idea: Instruments are classified by what vibrates: a solid body, a skin, a string, air, or electricity.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. If a note vibrates at 440 Hz, what is the frequency of the same note one octave higher?
Answer. 880 Hz.
Question two. How was the huge repertoire of medieval church chant mostly learned?
Answer. By heart, which took singers many years.
Question three. What happens when you press a guitar string exactly halfway along?
Answer. The note rises an octave in pitch.
Question four. In the Hornbostel-Sachs system, what is a drum with a stretched skin?
Answer. A membranophone.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
